I was in Kandahar Province. I served with third Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division, Mountain Infantry Division. So what the army had me do was, well, let me back up here a little bit. In history, in American history, when we pick up enemy POWs. Historically, it was pretty easy. I mean, in the Second World War, if you wore a German uniform or you wore a Japanese uniform, you wore a POW and we shoved you in the POW camp. If you weren't wearing a German or Japanese uniform, we let you go. In Afghanistan, same in Iraq, the battlefield is much more complex. The enemy is not wearing uniforms. And frequently, it wasn't exactly 100% clear. Was this person really an enemy Taliban? And therefore, we should put them in a POW camp, or were they just the farmer in the wrong place at the wrong time? and therefore we should let them go. So what the Army had me do was they assigned me to a brigade combat team, and I was the JAG for the brigade combat team, and my job specifically was to sort out when the infantry picked up Afghan nationals, review the evidence, review what the soldiers were saying, review with the circumstances of the pickup, and then make the decision. Is it more likely that not this person was enemy Taliban? send them to the POW camp or was here more likely than not just a civilian in the wrong place, therefore let them go. That was my decision. It was certainly not as easy at all. I mean, there were a lot of things that were very tough calls. If you have a moment, let me just give you a very, very small snippet or a very, very small example. I remember one of my first months on battlefield in Afghanistan. But they explained to me that we'll look at when they did a search and they found the number of things in his pockets. They found electric duct tape. They found batteries. They found wiring. Now that in and of itself in the United States or in the West is not really conducive to saying, you know, you're an enemy Taliban.
